questions.question: Q1. A quad has four motors rated 620 g thrust each and an all-up mass of 500 g. What is its thrust-to-weight ratio?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that uses one motor (620/500), not all four.
explanations.b: Incorrect — that is two motors' worth.

questions.question: Q2. Into which class does a thrust-to-weight ratio of 4.96 fall?

explanations.c: Correct — 3.0–5.0 is the agile freestyle band, where 4.96 sits.

questions.question: Q3. Using the quadratic thrust curve, what hover throttle does a TWR of 4.96 require?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that would need a much higher TWR.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 80% would mean a low TWR near 1.6.

questions.question: Q4. With a hover throttle of 44.9%, what is the control margin?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that is the hover throttle itself, not the reserve above it.
explanations.b: Incorrect — that ignores the exact hover point.
explanations.c: Correct — control margin = (1 − 0.449) × 100 = 55.1%, the throttle reserve above hover.
explanations.d: Incorrect — full range minus the hover throttle is 55.1%, not 100%.

questions.question: Q5. For a 500 g quadcopter, how much thrust must each of the four motors produce to hover?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that is the whole weight on one motor.
explanations.b: Incorrect — that splits the weight over two motors.
explanations.c: Correct — each of the four motors carries one quarter of the weight: 500 / 4 = 125 g.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that would be one eighth of the weight.

questions.question: Q6. With 620 g/motor and a 500 g empty mass, what is the maximum payload that keeps TWR at or above 2.0?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that understates the lift available.
explanations.b: Incorrect — that is the empty mass, not the payload.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 1240 g is the max all-up mass; subtract the 500 g empty mass to get the payload.

questions.question: Q7. As payload is loaded onto the craft, what happens to the hover throttle and control margin?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that is the effect of removing weight, not adding it.
explanations.b: Correct — added payload lowers TWR, so hover throttle = √(1/TWR) rises and the (1 − hover) margin shrinks.
explanations.c: Incorrect — they both depend on the changing TWR.
explanations.d: Incorrect — if hover throttle rises, the margin above it must shrink, not grow.

questions.question: Q8. Four 5″ (0.127 m diameter) propellers give what total actuator-disk area A = N·π(D/2)<sup>2</sup>?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that omits the factor of 4 motors and uses the wrong radius.
explanations.c: Incorrect — that is roughly the diameter, not the area.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that overestimates; recompute with radius 0.0635 m.

questions.question: Q9. Momentum theory puts the reference build's ideal hover efficiency near 11 g/W, yet the simulator's Thrust eff. chip reads about 2.65 g/W. What explains the fourfold gap?

answers.a: The simulator is miscalibrated and the theoretical figure is the correct one
answers.b: They are different quantities: the chip is an electrically measured full-throttle figure including copper, ESC and profile losses, while momentum theory is an idealised hover-power floor
answers.c: The difference is manufacturing tolerance on the figure of merit
answers.d: The chip reports watts per gram rather than grams per watt

explanations.a: Incorrect — both numbers are right for what they measure; the error is in comparing them.
explanations.b: Correct — the chip is maximum thrust divided by the electrical power drawn to make it, labelled `g/W @ full` in the Calculations card. Momentum theory ignores every electrical and profile loss and evaluates at hover, not full throttle.
explanations.c: Incorrect — a figure of merit spanning 0.55 to 0.75 could only move the ideal figure between roughly 9 and 13 g/W. It cannot account for a factor of four.
explanations.d: Incorrect — inverting the units would give about 0.38 W/g, not 2.65.

questions.question: Q10. Which two changes most improve a multirotor's hover efficiency (g/W)?

answers.b: Larger propeller disk and lower all-up mass
answers.c: Higher KV motors and a heavier frame
answers.d: Higher refresh rate and a smaller battery

explanations.b: Correct — a bigger disk lowers induced power for the same thrust, and a lighter craft needs less thrust (power scales as thrust^1.5), so both raise hover g/W. Note that only the disk-area effect shows on the simulator's full-throttle Thrust eff. chip, which is payload-independent.
explanations.c: Incorrect — a heavier frame lowers efficiency; KV alone does not set hover efficiency.
explanations.d: Incorrect — those affect control latency and endurance, not hover g/W directly.
